Coverage and enrichment testing

coverage_and_enrichment.Rmd

Overview

Setup 

library(multifactor)

# Wrangling
library(dplyr)

# Plotting
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(systemfonts)
library(ragg)

# Load demo data
set.seed(2612)
fox <- quickbrownfox()

# Define utility function
split_to_letters <- function(x) unique(
  unlist(
    strsplit(gsub(" ", "", x), split = ""),
    recursive = TRUE, use.names = FALSE
  )
)

Example Dataset: The Quick Brown Fox 

levels(fox)
#> $letter

Calculate coverage

We’ll need to generate some collection of letters as input data.

input <- split_to_letters("some collection of letters")

input
#>  [1] "s" "o" "m" "e" "c" "l" "t" "i" "n" "f" "r"

We can use the weave_coverage() function to calculate to what degree the input letters cover the words in our data set. This function behaves similarly to weave() but comes with an additional argument, .data. For now, let’s plug in our input letters:

res <- weave_coverage(
  x = fox, .path = letter ~ word, .data = input
)

res
#> A multifactor::linkmap data.frame S7_object: 32 rows.
#>    letter  word
#> 1       t   the
#> 2       h   the
#> 3       e   the
#> 4       q quick
#> 5       u quick
#> 6       i quick
#> 7       c quick
#> 8       k quick
#> 9       b brown
#> 10      r brown
#>  + 22 more rows. Use `print(n = ...)` to see more rows.
#> 
#> @ levels:   2 variables: 
#>  $ letter : 26 Levels: a ... z 
#>  $ word   :  8 Levels: brown ... the 
#> 
#> @ metadata: 5 variables: 
#> List of 5
#>  $ observed : logi  TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE FALSE TRUE ...
#>  $ set_count: int  2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 3 3 ...
#>  $ set_size : int  3 3 3 5 5 5 5 5 5 5 ...
#>  $ coverage : num  0.667 0.667 0.667 0.4 0.4 ...
#>  $ complete : logi  FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE ...

Now, let’s use a second set of letters that are explicitly part of the sentence:

input <- split_to_letters("jumps over")

input
#> [1] "j" "u" "m" "p" "s" "o" "v" "e" "r"
res <- weave_coverage(
  x = fox, .path = letter ~ word, .data = input
)

res
#> A multifactor::linkmap data.frame S7_object: 32 rows.
#>    letter  word
#> 1       t   the
#> 2       h   the
#> 3       e   the
#> 4       q quick
#> 5       u quick
#> 6       i quick
#> 7       c quick
#> 8       k quick
#> 9       b brown
#> 10      r brown
#>  + 22 more rows. Use `print(n = ...)` to see more rows.
#> 
#> @ levels:   2 variables: 
#>  $ letter : 26 Levels: a ... z 
#>  $ word   :  8 Levels: brown ... the 
#> 
#> @ metadata: 5 variables: 
#> List of 5
#>  $ observed : logi  FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE ...
#>  $ set_count: int  1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 2 2 ...
#>  $ set_size : int  3 3 3 5 5 5 5 5 5 5 ...
#>  $ coverage : num  0.333 0.333 0.333 0.2 0.2 ...
#>  $ complete : logi  FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE ...

Notice that the column named "complete" marks two particular words as complete now.

We can use the subset() method for linkmap to automatically filter for complete cases:

subset(res)
#> A multifactor::linkmap data.frame S7_object: 9 rows.
#>   letter  word
#> 1      j jumps
#> 2      u jumps
#> 3      m jumps
#> 4      p jumps
#> 5      s jumps
#> 6      o  over
#> 7      v  over
#> 8      e  over
#> 9      r  over
#> 
#> @ levels:   2 variables: 
#>  $ letter : 26 Levels: a ... z 
#>  $ word   :  8 Levels: brown ... the 
#> 
#> @ metadata: 5 variables: 
#> List of 5
#>  $ observed : logi  TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE ...
#>  $ set_count: int  5 5 5 5 5 4 4 4 4
#>  $ set_size : int  5 5 5 5 5 4 4 4 4
#>  $ coverage : num  1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1
#>  $ complete : logi  TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE ...
